evidence.note: Enumerated all src files, listed the simd spec dir, and read ~5 source files (decode.rs, runtime.rs, types.rs, spec.rs, main.rs) up front before editing — establishing the skeleton's structure.
Built, ran i32.json/block.json spec tests and the full suite, then grepped FAIL output to locate which MVP assertions were failing — grounding work in the harness output format.
Inspected wabt's opcode.h/opcode.def to cross-check the 0xFD SIMD sub-opcode space against the real WASM SIMD encoding before generating decode/exec tables — a strong level-8 orientation element.

Identified the concrete unimplemented/buggy functions (Call, CallIndirect, exec_numeric, Return draining bug, exec_load sign-extension, v128 lane accessor stubs) and inspected NumOp/SimdOp enums — accurate model of dispatch and the locked contract.
Grepped for Call/CallIndirect/Return/exec_numeric/exec_load/v128_get/v128_set/exec_one and re-read the SimdOp enum, mapping the value-stack dispatch structure it needed to slot SIMD into.

reasoning: The agent clearly cleared the level-5 bar: it read decode.rs/runtime.rs/types.rs/spec.rs, located value types and dispatch, identified every buggy/unimplemented function, and used the spec-test harness output. It reached into level 8 by cross-checking the 0xFD sub-opcode families against wabt's real encoding tables and inspecting the NumOp/SimdOp enums. It falls short of 8-10 because there is no clear evidence it inspected the actual spec JSON assertion structure (only ran the harness), it never explicitly enumerated the public items locked by spec.rs/main.rs, and it did not proactively surface the tricky semantic contracts (NaN canonicalization, saturation, laneidx/memarg layout) before coding. That places it between the 5 and 8 anchors, at 7.
